questions.question: What is a database index and why is it important?
questions.title: Database Indexes — What They Are and Why They Matter
questions.direct_answer: A **database index** is a data structure (typically B-tree) that speeds up data retrieval on a column. Like a book index, it lets the DB find rows without scanning the entire table. It speeds up SELECT but slows down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what indexes are and their trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking indexes only have benefits — not aware of write performance cost and storage overhead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the B-tree structure briefly and mention that primary keys are automatically indexed in all major databases

sections.title: What is an Index?
sections.content: Without an index, a database must scan every row in a table to find matching records (full table scan). An index is a sorted data structure built on one or more columns that allows the database to jump directly to matching rows, similar to how a book index works.

sections.title: Creating an Index
Key Points
sections.content:
- Index speeds up SELECT/WHERE/ORDER BY/JOIN on indexed column
- Index slows down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (index must be updated too)
- Primary key is automatically indexed in MySQL/PostgreSQL
- B-tree index: balanced tree — O(log n) lookup instead of O(n) full scan
- EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows whether query uses an index

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A database index is a data structure that speeds up data retrieval. Without an index, the database does a full table scan — checking every row. With an index on the column you are filtering by, the database can jump directly to the relevant rows. MySQL uses B-tree indexes by default, which provide O(log n) lookup. The trade-off is that indexes take up disk space and slow down writes because every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update the index. Primary key columns are always indexed automatically. You can use EXPLAIN before a query to see whether the query is using an index.

questions.question: When should you NOT create an index on a column?
questions.title: When Not to Create an Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: Avoid indexes on: **small tables** (full scan is faster), **high-write columns** (index overhead on every write), **low-cardinality columns** (few unique values like boolean), and **rarely queried columns**. Over-indexing wastes storage and hurts write performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of index trade-offs and when NOT to index
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing every column thinking it always helps — not knowing about write overhead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cardinality: a boolean column with 2 values has low cardinality — index is useless because you still touch 50% of rows

sections.title: When NOT to Index
sections.content:
- **Small tables**: full scan of 100 rows is faster than index lookup overhead
- **Low cardinality columns**: boolean/status columns (only 2-5 unique values) — index returns too many rows
- **High-write columns**: columns updated frequently — every write updates the index too
- **Rarely queried columns**: indexing has cost even if never used for filtering
- **Columns already covered**: if composite index (a, b) exists, indexing (a) alone is redundant

sections.title: The Index Trade-off
sections.content: Every index increases storage size and adds overhead to INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations. The database engine must keep all indexes synchronized with the data. For write-heavy tables or small tables, this overhead can outweigh the read benefits.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Indexes are not always beneficial. You should not index columns on small tables because the overhead of using an index lookup can actually be slower than just scanning 100 rows. Avoid indexing low-cardinality columns — a status column with values like active or inactive has only 2 values, so the index would still return half the table. High-write columns should not be over-indexed because every INSERT and UPDATE must update all relevant indexes. A good rule of thumb: index columns used frequently in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses, but do not index every column.

questions.question: What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
questions.title: Composite Index in SQL — Column Order Matters
questions.direct_answer: A **composite index** covers multiple columns: `INDEX(department, salary)`. The order of columns matters — the index is most effective for queries that filter on the **leftmost prefix** first. `WHERE department = 'IT'` uses the index; `WHERE salary > 50000` alone does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of composite index column order and leftmost prefix rule
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating INDEX(a, b) then querying only on b and expecting it to use the index
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the leftmost prefix rule clearly and how to design composite indexes based on query patterns

sections.title: Composite Index Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- Composite index is sorted by first column, then second within first, etc.
- Leftmost prefix rule: queries must filter on columns in order from left
- INDEX(a, b, c): queries on (a), (a,b), (a,b,c) use the index
- Query on (b) or (c) alone: index NOT used
- Design: put high-cardinality, most-filtered column first

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A composite index covers multiple columns and is sorted first by the leftmost column, then by subsequent columns within each leftmost value. The important rule is the leftmost prefix rule: for a composite index on department and salary, queries filtering on department alone or department and salary together will use the index. But a query filtering only on salary will not use this index because the index is sorted primarily by department. When designing composite indexes, put the column you filter on most frequently and with highest cardinality as the leftmost column.

questions.question: How do you use EXPLAIN to check if a SQL query uses an index?
questions.title: EXPLAIN in SQL — Checking Index Usage
questions.direct_answer: **EXPLAIN** (MySQL) or **EXPLAIN ANALYZE** (PostgreSQL) shows the query execution plan. Key fields: `type` (ALL = full scan, ref/range/const = index used), `key` (which index used), `rows` (estimated rows scanned). Look for `type=ALL` as a warning sign.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of query execution plan analysis
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing EXPLAIN exists or what the output means
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain specific EXPLAIN output fields: type ALL = bad, key column shows which index is used

sections.title: EXPLAIN Usage
sections.content:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000;

-- Key output columns:
-- type: ALL (full scan), range/ref/const (index used)
-- key: name of the index used (NULL = no index)
-- rows: estimated rows examined
-- Extra: 'Using index' = covering index (no table lookup)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `type=ALL`: full table scan — add an index if this is on a large table
- `type=range`: index used for range condition (BETWEEN, >, <)
- `type=ref`: index used for equality condition
- `type=const`: single row match (very fast)
- `key` column: shows which index was selected (NULL = no index used)
- `Extra: Using index` means covering index — all data from index, no table lookup

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: EXPLAIN is a SQL command you prepend to any SELECT query to see the execution plan without actually running the query. The most important thing to look at is the type column: if it says ALL, that means a full table scan — no index is being used. If it says range, ref, or const, the query is using an index. The key column shows which specific index was selected. The rows column shows how many rows the optimizer estimates it needs to examine. If you see type ALL on a large table with a query that runs frequently, that is a signal to add an index.

followup_questions: What does type=ALL mean in EXPLAIN output?
What is a covering index and what does 'Using index' mean in EXPLAIN?
How do you force a query to use a specific index in MySQL?

questions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and non-clustered index?
questions.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A **clustered index** determines the physical order of rows in the table — there can be only one per table (usually the primary key). A **non-clustered index** is a separate structure with pointers to the actual rows. MySQL InnoDB: PK is clustered; all others are non-clustered.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you can have multiple clustered indexes per table
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that InnoDB stores all data in the clustered index (the primary key IS the table structure)

rows: Requires extra step to follow pointer

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A clustered index defines the physical storage order of rows in the table. In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is the clustered index — the rows are physically stored in primary key order. There can be only one clustered index per table. A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree structure that contains the indexed column values and pointers back to the actual row locations. You can have multiple non-clustered indexes. Range queries on a clustered index are very efficient because consecutive rows are stored together on disk. Non-clustered index lookups require following a pointer to the actual row, which adds one extra step.

speakable_v2.hook: Clustered versus non-clustered index — one of them IS the table, and there can only ever be one.

beats.content: A clustered index determines the physical order of rows on disk. In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is the clustered index — rows are physically stored in primary key order. Because the data and the index are the same thing, primary key lookups are extremely fast, and range scans on the primary key are efficient because adjacent rows are stored next to each other on disk. You can only have one clustered index per table.

A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree structure that stores the indexed column values and pointers to the actual row locations. When the database uses a non-clustered index to find a row, it first navigates the index, then follows the pointer to the actual row — one extra step compared to a clustered lookup.

content: InnoDB: primary key is clustered — all other indexes are non-clustered
If you define no primary key, InnoDB creates a hidden row-id as the clustered index
Multiple non-clustered indexes are allowed per table

questions.question: When does a SQL query NOT use an index even if one exists?
questions.title: Cases Where SQL Index is Not Used
questions.direct_answer: Indexes are not used when: using functions on the indexed column (`WHERE YEAR(date) = 2024`), leading wildcard in LIKE (`WHERE name LIKE '%java'`), implicit type conversion, or when the optimizer decides a full scan is cheaper (very small table or low selectivity).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating an index but writing queries that bypass it unknowingly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate each case with a concrete example and the fix

sections.title: Index Bypass Examples
sections.content:
-- Index NOT used: function on indexed column
WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = 2024;
-- Fix: WHERE hire_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'

-- Index NOT used: leading wildcard
WHERE name LIKE '%java%';
-- Fix: use full-text index or LIKE 'java%'

-- Index NOT used: implicit type conversion
-- If id is INT but you pass a string
WHERE id = '123'; -- may skip index in some DBs

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Function on indexed column: index cannot be used directly
- Leading wildcard (%text): full table scan, B-tree cannot start from unknown prefix
- Implicit type conversion: can prevent index usage
- Low selectivity: optimizer may choose full scan if condition matches >20-30% of rows
- OR conditions: sometimes optimizer skips index for OR across columns
- NOT operators (<>, NOT IN): may prevent index use depending on DB

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: There are several common cases where an existing index is bypassed. Using a function on the indexed column prevents index usage because the index is built on raw column values, not computed values. A leading percent wildcard in LIKE means the database cannot use a B-tree index because it needs to know the prefix. Implicit type conversion — like comparing an integer column with a string value — can also prevent index usage. Finally, if the query matches a very high percentage of rows, the optimizer might decide a full table scan is actually faster than using the index. You can verify index usage with EXPLAIN.
